title: What Is TypeScript?
summary: TypeScript helps catch many code mistakes while you are writing JavaScript.
nestedConcepts: Types do not validate outside data

subtopics.title: JavaScript underneath
subtopics.explanation: TypeScript accepts JavaScript syntax and adds optional type features. Most JavaScript code can be used in a TypeScript project, then improved gradually. It is like adding labels to an existing set of tools instead of replacing them. Some newer JavaScript features still depend on the project’s build setup. For example, a JavaScript function can gain a parameter type without changing the overall way it is called. In practice, a type annotation can help a shared function communicate its accepted values.

subtopics.title: Types describe values
subtopics.explanation: A type describes what kind of value is expected. `let age: number = 20` says that `age` should hold a number. It is like labeling a container before putting an item inside. The checker can warn when code puts an incompatible value there. For example, type a price as number so accidental text assignment is reported during editing. In practice, a checker error is evidence of a mismatch, not proof of the best product behavior.

subtopics.title: Errors before running
subtopics.explanation: The TypeScript checker looks for mismatches while you work. It can catch many incorrect assumptions, such as calling a number like a function. It is like a proofreader who knows the rules of the document. It cannot catch every logic mistake or guarantee that a feature behaves as intended. For example, the checker may catch a missing field before a page is opened. In practice, a build tool may transpile syntax while the TypeScript checker separately verifies types.

subtopics.title: Compile step
subtopics.explanation: Browsers do not normally run TypeScript syntax directly. A build step removes type information and produces JavaScript for the browser or server. It is like translating a marked-up draft into a version the reader can use. A successful type check and a successful build are separate checks. For example, a build command must still run to turn TypeScript syntax into browser-ready JavaScript. In practice, validate form and API data before trusting a type declaration.

subtopics.title: Types do not validate outside data
subtopics.explanation: Types cannot prove that a network response contains the fields your app expects. Type annotations disappear when the program runs. It is like a label on a box that has not been opened. Validate outside data at runtime before relying on its shape. For example, validate a JSON response before treating it as a typed user record. In practice, adopt TypeScript gradually by checking one module boundary at a time.

foundations.overview: TypeScript is JavaScript with a system for describing the kinds of values your code expects. Its checker can find many mistakes before the program runs, then a build tool removes type syntax and produces JavaScript. Think of it like adding labels and a proofreader to a recipe. It helps developers reason about code, but it cannot guarantee the program has no bugs or validate server data by itself.
foundations.whyItMatters: TypeScript makes assumptions visible and catches many mismatches before execution. Knowing its limits helps teams use it as a safety aid without mistaking it for runtime validation.
commonUseCases: Add checking to an existing JavaScript project.
Describe the props a shared component accepts.
Catch mismatched values before the application runs.

commonMisconceptions.reality: It checks declared assumptions but cannot prove all program behavior or validate external data.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Browsers normally execute TypeScript annotations directly.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A build or runtime tool must handle TypeScript syntax for the chosen environment.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A successful type check means a production build will succeed.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Type checking and building are distinct steps and can fail for different reasons.

visualExplorer.caption: Watch how typed source becomes plain JavaScript the browser can run.

config.intro: Trace what happens when you compile and run a TypeScript file.

steps.name: Write typed code
steps.detail: You author app.ts with type annotations like (name: string) — JavaScript plus types.

steps.name: Type-check
steps.detail: tsc reads the types and reports any mismatches (wrong arguments, typos, possible null) before emitting anything.

steps.name: Erase types
steps.detail: If checking passes, tsc strips every type annotation — they have done their job.

steps.name: Emit JavaScript
steps.detail: tsc writes app.js: ordinary JavaScript with no trace of the types.

steps.name: Run anywhere
steps.detail: The browser or Node.js loads app.js — it never sees the original TypeScript.

interactiveExamples.title: Typed code runs as plain JavaScript
interactiveExamples.explanation: The types are erased; at runtime this is just a normal function call. The sandbox strips the types and runs the JS.

interactiveExamples.title: Structural typing in action
interactiveExamples.explanation: TypeScript accepts the object because its shape matches Point, not because of a name. At runtime it's a plain object.

codeLab.title: Add type annotations to a JavaScript function
codeLab.instructions: Annotate the parameters and return type of add so it only accepts numbers. The runtime behavior is identical; the goal is to type it. Calling add(2, 3) should log 5.
hints: Add the return type after the parameter list: function add(a: number, b: number): number.

keyTakeaways: TypeScript accepts JavaScript syntax and adds optional type features.
A type describes what kind of value is expected.
The TypeScript checker looks for mismatches while you work.
Browsers do not normally run TypeScript syntax directly.
Types cannot prove that a network response contains the fields your app expects.
